title: Medical Record Dedup
description: Hash-set on a normalized fingerprint — a single `for` pass over discovery pages, keying a Set on lowercased/whitespace-collapsed text so duplicate pages in different casing or spacing collapse to one; keep first, count the rest.

conversation.intro: How a conversation about deduping discovery production would actually play out — opposing counsel sent over 10,000 PDFs and a lot of them are obviously the same page in different scans. Each section has two parts: what you'd actually say out loud, and why that move matters. Tap a section to expand.

sections.title: 1. Restate & clarify
sections.prompt: Before touching code — pin down what 'duplicate' means here.
sections.say:
"Let me restate: I've got a list of pages, each with an `id` and a `text` body, and I need to dedupe them. Output is the kept ids (first occurrence wins) and a count of how many duplicates were removed. The catch is that 'duplicate' isn't strict equality — pages from different scans have inconsistent casing and whitespace, so 'Patient stable.' and 'patient   STABLE. ' should collapse to one record."

Clarifiers first:
• What counts as 'the same page' — exact text after casing/whitespace normalization, or fuzzy match (Levenshtein, MinHash, embedding similarity)? Fuzzy is a different algorithm entirely.
• Which whitespace transforms are safe to fold away? Lowercasing + collapsing runs of whitespace is safe for natural-language pages. Removing punctuation is more aggressive — risky if the documents are code or have meaningful punctuation.
• 'First occurrence wins' — first by input order, or first by id, or first by date? If pages come in scan-order and that happens to be chronological, first-by-input is what 'first occurrence' usually means.
• Should the kept id be returned as-is, or normalized? Almost always as-is — we normalize the COMPARISON key, not the records themselves.
• What's the dataset size? Tens of pages — `Set` is fine. Tens of millions — you'd want a bloom filter or external sort.
• Do I care about the COUNT of times each duplicate appeared, or just the total dup count? The current spec is a scalar; a per-fingerprint count would need a Map of fingerprint → count.
sections.why: The 'fuzzy vs exact' clarifier is the load-bearing one — if the answer is 'fuzzy', the whole algorithm changes and a hash Set won't work; you'd need MinHash + LSH or a vector embedding. The 'kept id is unnormalized' detail is the kind of subtle spec point that careless candidates miss — they normalize the entire record and lose the original casing of the id (which is wrong). The scale clarifier signals that you know hash-set dedup has a memory floor; for production-scale legal discovery you might mention bloom filters even if you don't implement them.

sections.title: 2. Brute force first (out loud)
sections.prompt: Name the obvious O(n²) solution before you discard it.
sections.say:
"The brute force is: for each page, scan the already-kept list and check if any kept page normalizes to the same fingerprint. If not, keep it; otherwise increment the duplicate counter. That's O(n²) in the number of pages, and within each comparison the normalization itself is O(L) for L characters — so really O(n² · L).

The optimization is obvious: instead of re-scanning the kept list, hash each page's fingerprint into a Set. Membership becomes O(1), so the whole dedup is O(n · L) — one normalization per page, one Set lookup per page. We trade O(n) space for the Set in exchange for O(n) instead of O(n²) time.

The other key choice: hash the NORMALIZED fingerprint, not the raw text. Raw text would not catch the casing/whitespace variants — 'Patient stable.' and 'patient STABLE.' would be two distinct Set entries. The whole point of the fingerprint is to fold those variants together BEFORE the hash sees them."
sections.why: Naming both the time-complexity win AND the structural choice (hash the fingerprint, not the raw) is what tells the interviewer you've thought about both dimensions. Many candidates jump to 'use a Set' without articulating that the SET KEY is itself a designed function — the lesson is hash-set + normalization, not hash-set alone. The factor-of-L in the complexity is also a senior touch; most candidates drop it and just say O(n), which is approximately right but misses that long pages do more work per comparison.

sections.title: 3. Spot the pattern — dedup-by-key with a Set
sections.prompt: What's the canonical structure and why first-wins?
sections.say:
"This is dedup-by-key — one of the most common hash-set patterns. The structure is:
• A `seen` Set of fingerprints.
• A `kept` array of the first-occurrence ids.
• A `dups` counter for the duplicates removed.
• A single `for` pass over the input.
• Per page: compute the fingerprint, check `seen.has`, branch on hit/miss.

The fingerprint is `p.text.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()` — three operations in a fixed order:
• `toLowerCase()` first because it's idempotent and cheap.
• `replace(/\s+/g, ' ')` collapses every run of one-or-more whitespace chars (spaces, tabs, newlines) into a single space — that handles the multi-space and embedded-tab cases.
• `trim()` at the end because the collapse step can leave a single leading/trailing space if the original had whitespace at the edges.

First-wins is enforced by the BRANCH ORDER inside the loop: on a hit, increment the counter and `continue` — DON'T push to `kept`, DON'T re-add to `seen`. On a miss, add to the Set AND push to `kept`. Because the Set is checked first and the kept-push is gated on a miss, only the very first occurrence ever ends up in `kept`. If you accidentally pushed on every iteration and only counted dups, `kept` would have every id and the dedup would be a no-op."
sections.why: Naming the three normalization steps in their fixed order is what proves you understand each one's role — they're not arbitrary, they compose. The 'trim AFTER collapse' detail is the load-bearing one: trim before collapse would leave embedded multi-spaces, and collapse alone leaves whitespace at the edges; only the trim-after-collapse order produces a tight, edge-clean fingerprint. The branch-order explanation is what makes first-wins fall out of the structure rather than feeling like an arbitrary choice.

sections.title: 4. Trace through examples
sections.prompt: Walk a few inputs to confirm the model before writing the loop.
sections.intro: "Let me trace a couple of inputs." Three cases cover the L3 input with two genuine duplicates that differ only in casing/whitespace, a degenerate all-unique case, and an exact-duplicate-only case to prove the fingerprint isn't doing anything special on identical input.

examples.input: [p1:'Patient stable.', p2:'patient   STABLE. ', p3:'MRI ordered.', p4:'Patient stable.']
examples.note: The L3 case. p2 differs from p1 only in casing and whitespace — fingerprint folds it to the same key. p4 is an exact duplicate of p1. Both should be counted, neither added to kept.
examples.trace:
seen={}, kept=[], dups=0
p1: 'Patient stable.' → fingerprint='patient stable.' → seen empty → seen.add → seen={'patient stable.'}, kept=[p1]
p2: 'patient   STABLE. ' → lc='patient   stable. ' → collapse=' patient stable. ' (wait — collapse INSIDE the string only; ' patient stable. ') → trim → 'patient stable.' → seen.has(key)=TRUE → dups++, continue. seen unchanged, kept unchanged. dups=1
p3: 'MRI ordered.' → fingerprint='mri ordered.' → seen.has=false → seen.add, kept=[p1,p3]
p4: 'Patient stable.' → fingerprint='patient stable.' → seen.has=TRUE → dups++. dups=2
return { kept:[p1,p3], dups:2 } ✓

examples.note: Degenerate all-unique case. Every page misses the Set; every id gets pushed. Proves the loop has no off-by-one when there are zero duplicates.
examples.trace:
seen={}, kept=[], dups=0
a: fingerprint='apple' → miss → seen={apple}, kept=[a]
b: fingerprint='banana' → miss → seen={apple,banana}, kept=[a,b]
c: fingerprint='cherry' → miss → seen={apple,banana,cherry}, kept=[a,b,c]
return { kept:[a,b,c], dups:0 } ✓

examples.input: [x:'same', y:'SAME', z:'same'] — three exact duplicates after lowercasing
examples.note: Exact-duplicates-only case (modulo casing). Proves first-wins: x is kept, y and z both count as duplicates because their fingerprint matches the one x added. Order matters — if input was [y, x, z] instead, kept would be [y].
examples.trace:
seen={}, kept=[], dups=0
x: fingerprint='same' → miss → seen={same}, kept=[x]
y: fingerprint='same' → HIT → dups++, continue. dups=1
z: fingerprint='same' → HIT → dups++. dups=2
return { kept:[x], dups:2 } ✓

sections.why: The L3 trace is the proof point for the normalization — without `toLowerCase` p2 stays distinct (different casing), and without `replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()` p2 still stays distinct (extra spaces and trailing space). All three normalization steps earn their keep on this single page. The all-unique case is the boring sanity check that nothing weird happens at empty-set boundaries. The third case demonstrates input-order-dependence — useful for the senior-tier interviewer who asks 'what if my input arrives in a different order?'.

sections.title: 5. Edge cases / failure modes
sections.prompt: What inputs would trip up a careless implementation?
sections.say:
"Edges worth flagging:
• Empty `pages` array → loop never fires, returns `{ kept: [], dups: 0 }`. Cheap and works.
• Whitespace-only pages — `'   \n\t '.replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()` = empty string. Two blank pages both fingerprint to `''` and the second is counted as a duplicate. Often that's what you want (blanks ARE duplicates of each other); sometimes you'd treat empty as a special case and skip dedup. Worth asking.
• Pages with the same text but different scan metadata (page number, OCR confidence, …) — the fingerprint only looks at `p.text`, so metadata variation doesn't break dedup. But if metadata MATTERS to identity, the fingerprint needs to include it (e.g. `${p.docId}:${p.text}`).
• Punctuation variation — 'Smith, John' vs 'Smith,John' (missing space inside the comma) → the collapse-whitespace step doesn't touch punctuation, so these stay distinct. If you wanted to also fold punctuation, you'd add `.replace(/[^a-z0-9 ]/g, '')` — but that's aggressive and would also fold meaningful differences like 'p.123' vs 'p123'.
• Unicode normalization — 'café' (composed é) vs 'cafe\u0301' (decomposed) are visually identical but compare unequal as strings. Adding `.normalize('NFKD')` before lowercasing handles that for accented Latin scripts. Worth flagging in a legal-tech context where European-language docs aren't unusual.
• Order-dependence — first-wins means the result depends on input order. If pages arrive un-ordered and you want deterministic output, sort by id first.
• Memory ceiling — the Set holds every distinct fingerprint. For 10M pages that's a lot of strings. A bloom filter would trade some false positives for O(1) memory; an external sort would trade time for streaming dedup.
• Hash collisions — JS Set uses real equality on the key strings, so no false-positive collisions. The fingerprint COULD have semantic collisions (different real pages that happen to lowercase to the same string) but that's a normalization-choice problem, not a hash problem."
sections.why: The Unicode normalization point is the kind of senior call-out that catches diversity of input — in real legal tech, you absolutely get composed-vs-decomposed forms mixed in OCR output. The 'fingerprint includes metadata if metadata matters' point is the general lesson: the identity function is part of the spec, not part of the implementation. The bloom filter mention is the right caveat for production scale — it shows you know the constant-memory alternative exists even though you wouldn't reach for it on a 100-page input.

sections.title: 6. Complexity & wrap-up
sections.prompt: How would you defend the complexity claim?
sections.say:
"Time is O(n · L) — one pass over n pages, with each page's fingerprint costing O(L) for L characters of text (the toLowerCase, the regex replace, the trim each scan the string once). The Set's `has` and `add` are O(L) for hashing the fingerprint key — same factor. So per-page work is O(L), and total is O(n · L).

Space is O(n · L) — the `seen` Set holds one fingerprint string per distinct page; in the worst case (no duplicates) that's n fingerprints averaging L chars each. The `kept` array adds O(n) ids on top. The `dups` counter is O(1).

If you wanted me to extend this:
• Per-fingerprint duplicate count → swap the Set for a `Map<fingerprint, { firstId, count }>`. Same loop shape, more reporting power.
• Bloom filter for huge datasets → false-positive rate ε, memory O(n log(1/ε)) bits regardless of L. Trade-off: you'd need a confirmation step on hits if accuracy matters.
• MinHash + LSH for near-duplicate detection → fingerprint becomes a sketch; 'similar' replaces 'identical'. The hash-set scaffolding survives — you'd just key on the sketch instead.
• Dedup-by-key on structured records → swap `p.text` for `p.email.toLowerCase()` or `${p.firstName}|${p.lastName}|${p.dob}` — same template, different fingerprint. This is the conflict-check pattern from another lesson on the sidebar.

The template is: hash-set keyed on a designed fingerprint + first-wins branch order. Anywhere you'd write `SELECT DISTINCT ON (lower(text)) * FROM pages ORDER BY id`, this is the in-memory equivalent."
sections.why: The MinHash/LSH connection is the senior-extension move — it shows you see exact-dedup as a special case of similarity dedup. The bloom filter mention demonstrates memory-vs-accuracy tradeoff awareness without committing to implementing it. The SQL `SELECT DISTINCT ON` analogy is the right anchor for the rusty-engineer audience — anyone who's written Postgres recognizes the pattern, which makes that the durable recall handle.

walkthrough.intro: Step through dedup-by-normalized-fingerprint on real discovery pages. The state panel shows the `seen` Set, the running `kept` array, the `dups` counter, and the current page's text → fingerprint transformation. Watch how the three-stage normalization (lowercase, collapse \\s+, trim) folds casing/whitespace variants together BEFORE the Set sees them.

examples.label: L3 input: 4 pages, 2 are duplicates of p1
three exact duplicates (casing only) → first wins

trace: yield { line: 4, label: 'init — seen empty Set, kept empty, dups=0, ' + pages.length + ' pages to process', state: { pages, seen: [], kept: [...kept], dups } };

yield { line: 9, label: 'page#' + i + ' ' + p.id + ' → lowercase=\'' + lower + '\' → collapse=\'' + collapsed + '\' → trim=\'' + key + '\'', state: { pages, seen: [...seen], kept: [...kept], dups, i, page: p, lower, collapsed, key } };
yield { line: 10, label: 'seen.has(\'' + key + '\') → HIT — dups++ → ' + dups + ', skip (kept unchanged)', state: { pages, seen: [...seen], kept: [...kept], dups, i, page: p, key, branch: 'hit' } };

yield { line: 12, label: 'miss — seen.add(\'' + key + '\'), kept.push(\'' + p.id + '\') → kept=' + JSON.stringify(kept), state: { pages, seen: [...seen], kept: [...kept], dups, i, page: p, key, branch: 'miss' } };
yield { line: 14, label: 'return { kept: ' + JSON.stringify(kept) + ', dups: ' + dups + ' }', state: { pages, seen: [...seen], kept: [...kept], dups, returns: JSON.stringify(result) } };

reference.approach: Hash set on a normalized text fingerprint
notes: Normalize before comparing. Raw `===` treats 'Patient stable.' and 'patient   STABLE.' as different, so the duplicate slips through. The fingerprint folds casing and whitespace away first.
`replace(/\s+/g, ' ')` collapses any run of spaces, tabs, or newlines into a single space; the trailing `.trim()` strips leading/trailing whitespace the collapse leaves behind.
Keep the FIRST occurrence: on a hit, `continue` past the page without overwriting `seen` or `kept`. Pushing on every miss (not every page) is what makes 'first wins' hold.
Time O(n·L), Space O(n·L) — one pass over n pages; each fingerprint costs O(L) to build and hash; Set holds up to n strings of avg length L.

questions.q: Why normalize the text into a fingerprint before comparing pages?
options: `Set.has` hashes the input via `Object.prototype.toString`, which is case-sensitive, so the key must be pre-lowered
Raw equality (`===`) treats different casing/whitespace as distinct, so real duplicates would not be caught
Storing the raw text in a Set would retain reference identity, so equal-by-value strings would still miss
`replace(/\s+/g, ' ')` returns a value that `Set` accepts; the unmodified `text` would be coerced to `[object String]`
questions.explain: 'Patient stable.' and 'patient   STABLE.' are the same page; only after lowercasing and collapsing whitespace do they hash to the same key.

questions.q: Why use a Set of fingerprints rather than re-scanning `kept` for each page?
options: `kept.includes(key)` does deep equality on objects, which would mis-match string fingerprints
Set membership (`has`) is O(1), so the whole dedup is O(n) instead of O(n^2)
Iterating `kept` mid-loop would mutate the index and skip pages
A Set can hold arbitrary objects as keys; arrays can only hold primitive types
questions.explain: Scanning the kept list for every page is O(n^2). A Set gives constant-time membership, keeping the pass linear.

questions.q: How does the code guarantee it keeps the FIRST occurrence of a duplicate?
options: `Set.add` returns the prior value on collision, which is used to overwrite `kept[i]` with the earlier id
On a Set hit it increments the count and `continue`s without overwriting `seen` or `kept`
It checks `seen.size` before the push and only appends when the size grew
It compares the page's index against `seen.size` and keeps whichever is lower
questions.explain: The first time a fingerprint is seen, its id is pushed. Every later match just counts and skips, so the original id stays.

questions.q: What does `replace(/\s+/g, ' ')` do to the text 'a\t b\n c'?
options: Collapses every run of whitespace to a single space, giving 'a b c'
Replaces only the first whitespace run
questions.explain: `\s+` matches any run of one-or-more whitespace chars (spaces, tabs, newlines); the global flag replaces each run with one space.

exercises.prompt: Normalize a page's text into a fingerprint: lowercase, collapse whitespace runs to one space, trim. Fill the regex and the trim call.
Dedupe by fingerprint using a Set: on a hit, count and skip; otherwise record and keep. Fill the Set methods so the duplicate is counted and only the first id is kept.

L3.prompt: Discovery produced duplicate pages with inconsistent whitespace/casing. Dedupe by a normalized fingerprint (lowercase, collapse runs of whitespace to one space, trim). Keep the first occurrence's id; report kept ids and how many duplicates were removed.
hints: Build the fingerprint with `text.toLowerCase().replace(/\s+/g, ' ').trim()` — that folds away casing and whitespace differences.
Track seen fingerprints in a Set; on a hit, increment a duplicate counter and `continue`.
On a miss, add the fingerprint to the Set and push the page id to the kept list — that keeps the first occurrence.
